newsitem.title: UK: London platinum, palladium prices soar.
newsitem.headline: London platinum, palladium prices soar.

text.p: Prices of rare precious metals platinum and palladium leapt up on Thursday on fears there could be strike next month at Russia's huge Norilsk production facility in Arctic Siberia.
"The pressure has been building for some time but the strike news was the last straw," a dealer said.
Later prices eased as speculators took their profits but at the London morning fixing platinum was at $393.50 per ounce, up $10.00 and its highest fix since September 9, 1996.
Sister metal palladium jumped $7.00 to fix at $157.00, last seen on July 11, 1995.
At 1530 GMT platinum was indicated at $390.50/$391.50 still up $8.50 and palladium was $7.45 ahead at $152.50/$153.50.
Gold was swept along, too, to reach its highest fixing since January 3 this year at $360.00.
"There has been a lot of short-covering (in gold) by the U.S. investment funds on the back of the palladium price," a dealer said.

A union official at Russia's cash-strapped Norilsk facility where workers have not been paid since October said this week a strike could begin on March 15. But a spokesman of the plant said the comment was "premature".
Even so, the market noted the threat. "A strike at Norilsk would cause major problems for consumers," one dealer said.
Another added, "The speculators jumped in when they read that. They saw a fundamentally tight market with a rising price and said 'let's go'."
Russia is the leading exporter of platinum after South Africa, and the largest exporter of palladium. Japan is by far the largest consumer of both metals.

Platinum is used in jewellery, electronics, many chemical applications and as part of the mix of metals in autocatalysts which remove toxic gases from car exhaust fumes. Palladium is used in autocatalysts, electronics and dental alloys.
Market interest grew earlier this year when it became clear that a delayed start to negotiations on 1997 exports between Russian and the Japanese trade houses could disrupt supplies.
Talks have not begun yet and market insiders are forecasting shipments might not begin until May.
Analyst Jeremy Coombs at Johnson Matthey, the world's leading refiner of the metals, said Japan's consumption of platinum and palladium was huge in 1995
Importers were contractually obliged to take the same quantities from Russia last year despite an economic downturn that cut demand for platinum and palladium bearing goods.
But now surplus stocks are being used up which is being reflected in borrowing rates for palladium in Europe doubling in the past few weeks, he said.
"There is also a premium of $5-$6 on sponge grade material which proves that Russia has not been shipping metal," Coombs added.
Sponge grade is the preferred type of palladium for most industrial use and normally has a premium to ingot of about $1.
Dealers said the price may not have peaked yet. "If the Russians get their export licences they could make spot sales and the price could suddenly correct," one dealer said.
"But equally if they cannot make up for lost exports, you could expect further rises," he added. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 7729
